body: The poignant “Leave It Alone” saw the arrival of a female string quartet that periodically reappeared throughout the set — and also the intriguing use of a polyrhythm complex enough that you had to remind yourself it was your mind that was out of time, not the band itself. After this, Williams took time out between songs to celebrate the audience’s approval of all the “Petals for Amor” songs, like “Leave It Alone,” that had provided the majority of the set thus far, half-seriously remarking that the whole tour was a “Trojan horse” to get to finally play that material.

Among the “Petals for Armor” songs in the set that were performed without comment: “Dead Horse,” a song understood to be about her relationship with former husband Chad Gilbert. As fans had noted, she took it out of the set for three concerts following his death last month, apparently out of respect, but it’s back in, because history is history, and relational trauma transformed into a sing-along dance track is always a recipe for concert success.

articles.title: Sebastian Stan Doesn’t Know How ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Turned Out, But Says It’s ‘Probably Heartbreaking’: ‘We’ll See Who Makes It’
articles.summary: Sebastian Stan, who suited back up as the Winter Soldier, Bucky Barnes, for the forthcoming “Avengers: Doomsday,” recently revealed he hasn’t actually seen the movie yet — but expects it to be “heartbreaking.” “I haven’t seen the movie, and I don’t know how it turned out,” the actor admitted while…
body: While fans have interpreted Stan’s comments as a tip that more than a few of the beloved characters will be killed off in the “Avengers: Endgame” follow-up, the actor is the latest “Doomsday” cast member to confess that they don’t really know what to expect when it comes to the film’s narrative. Recently, Alan Cumming, who will reprise his role as the mutant superhero Nightcrawler, told SiriusXM: “To be honest, I don’t fully understand the plot.” (He first appeared as the character in 2003’s “X2: X-Men United.”) Cumming also noted that most of his scenes were shot “in front of a blue screen.”

Perhaps the confusion stems from the unfinished script the co-directors, Joe and Anthony Russo, shot the film with. “We always view the script as a living organism,” Joe told the Associated Press last month. “We’re improvisation-based, rehearsal-based directors. We like to see what the actors bring to the characters, and sometimes you don’t get the actors until a few days or few weeks before you shoot them. And a lot of the time, that’s when the magic happens.”

articles.title: Patreon Co-founder Sam Yam Partners with Podcaster Chloe Shih After Joining OpenAI’s Creator Initiative (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Patreon co-founder Sam Yam joined OpenAI last month to lead its creator initiative — and he’s already got his first project set up. Yam is partnering with podcast host Chloe Shih, who launched her podcast “Office Drama” earlier this year, on a new series to explore how technology can help those…
body: Shih will also use OpenAI’s Dots, its always-on AI agent and competitor to Meta’s Muse that it unveiled during its DevDay showcase last month, to help produce the project.

Yam, who co-founded Patreon as a creator-focused monetization platform in 2013 and served as its president, announced on X last month that he would join OpenAI as its head of creator product — and that Patreon’s heads of product and engineering would join him. The exits followed Patreon’s layoffs in July, when it pink-slipped roughly 20% of its staff.
Yam wrote in a Sept. 22 X thread that he loved creators’ “relentless dedication to the craft” and was excited to help them bring “many more of their ideas to life.”

“I believe human creativity is paramount,” he wrote. “It allows us to see ourselves reflected in the world around us and drives authentic connections — and at the heart of it is a universal desire to be seen as we are and know that we are not alone.”

articles.title: Questlove Reflects on the Power of Vulnerability and Being a Trailblazer: ‘I Gotta Be the Change I Want to Be’
articles.summary: More than 30 years into his career, Questlove is still open to change. The Roots frontman and multi-hyphenate has performed in Jimmy Fallon’s in-house band for over a decade, was a producer on the “Hamilton” cast album, is an adjunct professor at NYU, hosts a podcast and has written eight books.
body: Questlove sat down with Variety ‘s Jem Aswad to discuss embracing vulnerability and being a changemaker at the Variety Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage presented by OUTFRONT.

Questlove said he would have called Prince his North Star when he first entered the industry. Now, with the “residue” of his Earth, Wind & Fire documentary still lingering, he said he feels like a new artist. “I’m still learning what the Questlove brand is,” he said. “I joke that this is Questlove 3.0 happening right now.”

“Earth, Wind & Fire (To Be Celestial vs That’s the Weight of the World)” was released in June. Directed and produced by Questlove, the documentary explores the band’s career and that of its founder, Maurice White. While creating the documentary, he read many of the books White read during the band’s genesis, which inspired his current approach to creativity.

articles.title: Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?
articles.summary: The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism. Hollywood is sending a clear message: it’s a friend of tech.
body: The enormous pull of the tech industry – including its many trillions of dollars, oversized influence on politics and heavily pushed algorithms and AI products – means Hollywood is not alone in courting its wealth, but it has intensified the historic tension between art and commerce in the entertainment business. Technology that augments the human experience may be a compelling narrative subject, but this year brings a trio of films about the gurus responsible for the industry’s false promises.

Time will tell how severely these films will affect the credibility of their subjects, but recent surveys indicate young Americans are already turning on giants such as Zuckerberg, Musk, and Altman. It seems as if these projects are taking advantage of a rising tide of tech scepticism rather than forging it themselves. What’s more noteworthy is how the films coincide with the widespread devaluing of films as art by corporations and their products.
points: The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism.
Hollywood is sending a clear message: it’s a friend of tech.

articles.title: Samuel L. Jackson Confirms His Next Marvel Movie As Nick Fury (It's Not Doomsday)
articles.summary: In an interview, Nick Fury actor Samuel L. Jackson revealed when his character will be making his big-screen return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
body: The upcoming superhero mashup picture "Avengers: Doomsday" already boasts an impressively large cast, culling actors from across the Marvel Cinematic Universe and beyond to team up and fight Dr. Doom (Robert Downey Jr.). Thanks to all the hype behind it, even the most casual readers likely know that Chris Evans will be back as the first Captain America, Chris Hemsworth will be returning as Thor, and so, so many others will join them. The real coup, however, is that "Doomsday" will feature many actors from the X-Men movie universe, finally paying off several X-Men cameos in films like "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," "The Marvels," and "Deadpool & Wolverine."

One notable absence from "Doomsday" is Samuel L. Jackson, who played the stalwart super-agent Nick Fury across multiple MCU shows and movies since his debut in the credits stinger of 2008's "Iron Man." Fury, as all Marvel fans can tell you, is the one responsible for assembling the Avengers into a superhero team in the first place. His centrality to the MCU cannot be understated.

articles.title: Post your questions for Celia Imrie
articles.summary: From Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to begin. Celia Imrie has had such a varied career, it’s hard to know where you might know her best from.
body: Maybe you know her as Mrs Quickly, the ghastly would-be stepmother in Nanny McPhee. Or maybe you first encountered her in Upstairs, Downstairs, To the Manor Born, Bergerac, Lovejoy or The Darling Buds of May, or as Claudia Bing, the magnificently awful PR rival of Jennifer Saunders’ Edina in Absolutely Fabulous.

More recently, she returned as Una in Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy; joined Helen Mirren, Pierce Brosnan and Ben Kingsley in The Thursday Murder Club; and popped up in The Diplomat. Then, of course, there was The Celebrity Traitors. Imrie entered the castle as a Faithful, survived being chained up in a wooden cabin, and accidentally farted while doing so – instantly producing the Guardian’s No 2 TV moment of the year – and eventually got murdered in plain sight by Alan Carr.

Now she’s back as in (yes, it’s nearly that time already) Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint, alongside John Bradley as a Christmas-hating model-soldier painter sentenced to community service at a struggling retirement home, where he somehow ends up directing a chaotic production of A Christmas Carol. Richard E Grant and Jim Broadbent are along for the festive ride, too.

articles.title: An Emotional Andrew Scott and ‘Elsinore’ Kick Off a Starry 2026 London Film Festival
articles.summary: The Irishman was joined by co-stars Olivia Colman, Luke Thompson, Billie Piper and Johnny Flynn, as well as the real-life influences on Ian Charleson's life before his death from AIDS in 1990.
body: Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman and the cast of Elsinore have officially kicked off the 2026 BFI London Film Festival, and the opener couldn’t have been more fitting.

Described by Thompson as “a real love letter to theater,” the film is based on the life of Ian Charleson. It follows the actor’s final weeks before his death from AIDS playing Hamlet at London’s National Theatre in the 1990s. The glitzy gala at this year’s London Film Fest was especially poignant for audiences, with the Royal Festival Hall just a stone’s throw from the NT.

“I can’t tell you how extraordinary this feels for us to be here,” began Scott — also a producer on the film — on stage. “[And] how grateful I feel to play this extraordinary person. It was an extraordinary honor to play this person who was so wickedly funny and joyful and talented and charming and beautiful,” he continued. “It was the honor of a lifetime.”

articles.title: Marilyn Monroe and Sydney Sweeney Are Related
articles.summary: The actresses are ninth cousins, once removed. They share a mutual ancestor, Ezra Perry (c. 1625–1689), who was an early English settler in Sandwich, Massachusetts.
body: Marilyn Monroe and Sydney Sweeney are related, according to a new study by MyHeritage.

At the 2026 Santa Barbara Film Festival, Sweeney also wore a vintage Ceil Chapman gown that resembled that of the look Monroe sported on the cover of LIFE magazine in April 1952, furthering tendencies to point out their likeness.

“People have always drawn parallels between Sydney Sweeney and Marilyn Monroe, but seeing their paths align on a deeper level inspired us to look for a real bond in the MyHeritage archives,” said Roi Mandel, director of research at MyHeritage, in a statement. “Uncovering their shared branch was incredible, it’s a powerful reminder that humanity is one vast family tree, and when we dig deep, we uncover how remarkably interconnected we all are.”

The Emmy nominee has never portrayed Monroe onscreen, though many actresses have. Among those are Ana de Armas in Blonde and Michelle Williams for My Week with Marilyn, whom both earned Oscar nominations for their respective performances.

articles.title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
articles.summary: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump. Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts.
body: Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.

The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.
points: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump.

articles.title: ‘The Louis Theroux Podcast’ to Double Spotify Output, Unveils Season 9 Guests (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Hollywood A-lister Judd Apatow, Monty Python legend Eric Idle and the former star of Theroux's 'The Most Hated Family in America,' Megan Phelps-Roper, will join the British broadcaster on the next installment.
body: Theroux fans, you’re in luck: The beloved documentarian is doubling his podcast output.

The Hollywood Reporter can reveal that Spotify and Theroux’s Mindhouse Studios are set to release twice as many episodes of The Louis Theroux Podcast, with season nine launching Oct. 14 and new installments arriving weekly.

British writer and broadcaster Jon Ronson, poet and performer John Cooper Clarke, actor and former footballer Vinnie Jones, author and activist Naomi Klein and Megan Phelps-Roper (who previously featured on his documentary The Most Hated Family in America ) will also sit down to talk with Theroux, alongside further guests still to be announced.

Previous guests of the popular pod include Florence Pugh, Gary Lineker, Steve Coogan, Malala Yousafzai, Bella Ramsey, Sharon Stone, Barry Keoghan and more, as Theroux leans further into the format that has become a natural home for his particular style of interviewing: long-form, freewheeling conversations with people whose lives and work spark his curiosity.
